source_refs.note: Book p. 222: 12.2.1 lim (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) = n a^(n-1): Case 1 (n a positive integer, factorization) and Case II (n = -m a negative integer, reduced to Case 1).

items.title: 12.2.1 Lim_{x->a} (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) = n a^(n-1) where n is a non-zero integer and a > 0

blocks.text: This important limit holds for every non-zero integer \(n\) and \(a > 0\):

blocks.text_alt: limit as x approaches a of (x to the power n minus a to the power n) over (x minus a) equals n times a to the power n minus 1

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is this limit needed? Substituting \(x = a\) gives \(\frac{a^{n}-a^{n}}{a-a} = \frac{0}{0}\), so it cannot be found directly. The result gives the answer at once, without factorizing every time.
For \(n = 2\) you can see it yourself: \(\frac{x^{2}-a^{2}}{x-a} = x + a\), which tends to \(2a = 2a^{2-1}\).
This limit is also the first step towards the derivative of \(x^{n}\), which you will meet in the next unit.
Case 1
Suppose \(n\) is a positive integer. By substituting \(x = a\), we get \(\left(\frac{0}{0}\right)\) form, so we make factors as follows:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where does this factorization come from? Check small powers:
\[x^{2}-a^{2} = (x-a)(x+a)\]
\[x^{3}-a^{3} = (x-a)(x^{2}+ax+a^{2})\]
In general, multiply \((x-a)\) by the long bracket: every middle term appears once with \(+\) and once with \(-\) and cancels. Only \(x^{n}\) and \(-a^{n}\) are left. In the bracket the powers of \(x\) go down by one and the powers of \(a\) go up by one, so there are exactly \(n\) terms.
Therefore, cancelling the common factor \((x - a)\) and then substituting \(x = a\):

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why does every term become \(a^{n-1}\)? In each term the two powers add up to \(n-1\), for example \(a^{2}\,a^{n-3} = a^{2+n-3} = a^{n-1}\). The bracket has \(n\) terms, so the sum is \(n\) copies of \(a^{n-1}\), i.e. \(na^{n-1}\).
Case II
Suppose \(n\) is a negative integer (say \(n = -m\)) where \(m\) is a positive integer. Now,

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why this rearrangement? A negative power is a reciprocal: \(x^{-m} = \frac{1}{x^{m}}\). Taking the L.C.M. gives \(\frac{a^{m}-x^{m}}{x^{m}a^{m}}\). We then write \(a^{m}-x^{m} = -(x^{m}-a^{m})\) so that the expression \(\frac{x^{m}-a^{m}}{x-a}\) of Case 1 appears, with the positive integer \(m\).
\(\therefore\)

\[\lim_{x\to a}\dfrac{x^{n}-a^{n}}{x-a}\]
\[= \lim_{x\to a}\left(\dfrac{-1}{x^{m}a^{m}}\right)\]
\[\quad \times \lim_{x\to a}\left(\dfrac{x^{m}-a^{m}}{x-a}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{-1}{a^{m}a^{m}}\,(ma^{m-1}) \quad \text{(by Case 1)}\]
\[= -ma^{-m-1}\]

\[\therefore\ \lim_{x\to a}\dfrac{x^{n}-a^{n}}{x-a} = na^{n-1}\]
\[\because\ n = -m\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two small steps the book leaves out:
1. \(\dfrac{ma^{m-1}}{a^{m}a^{m}} = ma^{m-1-2m} = ma^{-m-1}\).
2. With \(n = -m\): \(na^{n-1} = (-m)a^{-m-1}\), which is exactly what we found.
So the same formula holds for negative integers too. For negative \(n\) we need \(a \ne 0\) (we divide by \(a^{m}\)); the book takes \(a > 0\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Before using the result, make the question match its shape exactly: the same power \(n\) on \(x\) and on the constant, and the denominator \(x - a\) with the same \(a\). Write constants as powers first, e.g. \(8 = 2^{3}\), \(\frac{1}{4} = 2^{-2}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\lim_{x\to a}\frac{x^{n}-a^{n}}{x-a} = na^{n-1}\) for every non-zero integer \(n\).
2. Case 1 (\(n > 0\)): factorize \(x^{n}-a^{n}\), cancel \(x - a\), substitute: \(n\) equal terms.
3. Case II (\(n = -m < 0\)): rewrite with positive powers and use Case 1.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing the answer as \(na^{n}\) or \(na^{n+1}\). The power goes down by one: \(na^{n-1}\).
2. Using the result when the denominator is \(a - x\). Since \(a - x = -(x - a)\), the answer changes sign.
3. Forgetting to write the constant as a power with the same exponent, e.g. using \(a = 8\) in \(\frac{x^{3}-8}{x-2}\) instead of \(8 = 2^{3}\), \(a = 2\).
